units.t: Training Your Attention.
Part one. Where your mind goes.
Let's start with a quick question.
Over the last minute or so, before this lesson began, where was your mind?
Was it on the road, the footpath, the thing in front of you?
Or was it somewhere else entirely, replaying a conversation or planning tonight's dinner?
If it was somewhere else, you're in very good company.
In 2010, two Harvard psychologists, Matthew Killingsworth and Daniel Gilbert, ran one of the biggest studies of everyday attention ever done.
They built an iPhone app that pinged people at random moments through the day.
Each time, it asked three things.
What are you doing right now?
Are you thinking about something other than what you're doing?
And how happy do you feel?
More than two thousand adults took part, and the answers added up to a quarter of a million moments.
The headline result was striking.
People's minds were wandering about forty-seven per cent of the time.
Nearly half of waking life, spent somewhere other than where they actually were.
The only activity where minds wandered noticeably less often was making love.
The second finding was even more interesting.
People were generally less happy when their minds were wandering, even when they drifted to pleasant things.
The researchers summed it up in the title of their paper.
A wandering mind is an unhappy mind.
Now, that doesn't mean daydreaming is bad.
Mind wandering helps us plan, imagine and solve problems in the background.
The point is that it happens far more than we realise, and usually without our permission.
So why does attention drift so easily?
One helpful way to think about it is that your attention has two bosses.
One is you, deciding what to focus on.
The other is your brain's built-in alarm system, which constantly scans for anything new, moving or loud.
For our ancestors, a rustle in the grass might have been a predator, so the alarm system usually wins.
A phone buzzing in your pocket sets off exactly the same machinery.
There's also a simple matter of fuel.
Holding focus on one thing takes steady effort, and the effort gets harder the longer you go without a break.
Drift isn't a character flaw.
It's the default setting.
The good news is that defaults can be nudged, and that's where we're heading.
But first, let's deal with the most popular myth about attention.
Part two. The multitasking myth.
Plenty of us are proud of being good multitaskers.
Answering emails during a meeting.
Scrolling through the news while the kids tell us about their day.
It feels efficient.
The research says something different.
For most tasks that need thinking, the brain doesn't really do two things at once.
It switches back and forth between them, very quickly.
And every switch has a small cost.
In 2001, the psychologists Joshua Rubinstein, David Meyer and Jeffrey Evans measured this.
They had people flip between different kinds of tasks and timed them carefully.
Every switch cost time, and the costs grew as the tasks got more complicated.
Each cost might be a fraction of a second.
But David Meyer has suggested that across a busy day, switching can eat up as much as forty per cent of someone's productive time.
There's a hidden cost too.
A business researcher called Sophie Leroy gave it a name in 2009.
She called it attention residue.
When you leave one task unfinished and jump to another, part of your mind stays stuck on the first one.
You're physically on task two, but a slice of your attention is still back on task one, which makes you worse at both.
What about people who multitask all the time?
Surely they get good at it.
In 2009, a team at Stanford University led by Eyal Ophir, working with Clifford Nass and Anthony Wagner, tested exactly that.
They compared heavy media multitaskers with light ones.
The heavy multitaskers were worse at ignoring distractions.
And to the researchers' surprise, they were also worse at switching between tasks, the very skill you'd expect them to have practised.
This matters most of all behind the wheel.
The psychologist David Strayer, at the University of Utah, has spent years studying drivers on the phone.
One of his most important findings is that hands-free calls are not much safer than holding the phone, as far as distraction goes.
The problem isn't mainly your hands.
It's your attention being pulled into the conversation.
That's worth remembering next time a tricky call comes in on the drive home.
Our screens make all this harder.
Gloria Mark, a researcher at the University of California, Irvine, has timed how long office workers stay on one screen before switching.
Back in 2004, it was about two and a half minutes.
In her more recent studies, the average was around forty-seven seconds.
We're not just being interrupted by others.
More and more, we interrupt ourselves.
Part three. Small habits that help.
So what actually helps?
The first habit is to single-task on purpose.
Pick one thing and give it a short, protected block of time.
Twenty-five minutes works well for many people.
That's the idea behind the Pomodoro technique, created by an Italian university student called Francesco Cirillo in the late 1980s, and named after his tomato-shaped kitchen timer.
When the block ends, take a short break, then go again.
The second habit is to move temptation out of reach.
Distractions win most easily when they cost nothing.
So add a little friction.
Put your phone in another room, or at least face down and on silent.
Turn off the notifications you don't truly need.
Close the email tab while you write.
You're not relying on willpower.
You're changing the setting so willpower isn't needed as often.
The third habit is to finish cleanly before you switch.
Remember attention residue.
If you have to leave a task, take ten seconds to note exactly where you're up to and what the next step is.
Sophie Leroy's later research found that a quick plan like this helps your mind let go, so you can give the next thing your full attention.
A close cousin of this habit is batching.
Instead of answering every message the moment it lands, check them at set times, say once an hour, or at the top of each hour.
Each check becomes one planned switch instead of dozens of small unplanned ones.
Most messages can wait fifty minutes without anyone noticing.
And if something is truly urgent, people usually find a way to call.
The fourth habit is one you might be doing right now.
Take a proper break outside.
In 2008, Marc Berman, John Jonides and Stephen Kaplan, at the University of Michigan, sent people on walks.
Some walked through a leafy arboretum.
Others walked along busy city streets.
Afterwards, the nature walkers did noticeably better on a demanding memory and attention test, improving by about twenty per cent.
The street walkers didn't improve much at all.
Their idea is that busy streets keep grabbing your attention, while trees, water and sky let it rest and refill.
Finally, here's a small attention exercise you can do by ear.
If you're driving, keep your eyes and focus on the road, and simply treat the road as your anchor.
If you're walking, pick something simple to rest your attention on, like the sound of your footsteps.
For the next minute or so, whenever you notice your mind has drifted, quietly say to yourself, wandering, and gently come back.
That's the whole exercise.
The moment of noticing isn't a failure.
It's the actual training.
Every time you catch the drift and return, you're strengthening the same skill you'll use at your desk.
Let's recap.
Our minds wander almost half the time, and multitasking is really rapid switching, with a real cost in time and attention.
The fixes are small and practical.
Do one thing at a time, add friction to distractions, finish cleanly before you switch, and give your attention regular rest, ideally somewhere green.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. In the Killingsworth and Gilbert study, roughly how much of the time were people's minds wandering?
Answer. About forty-seven per cent, nearly half the time.
Question two. What did Sophie Leroy call the part of your mind that stays stuck on an unfinished task?
Answer. Attention residue.
Question three. In the Michigan study, which walk improved people's attention more, the city streets or the arboretum?
Answer. The walk through the leafy arboretum.
That's the end of Training Your Attention. Well focused. See you on the next one.
